# Problem 1

First we load our data and necessary libraries.
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")



```

This dataset `ny_noaa` shows the climate, including the amount of precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth, and some identification variables like id and date. There are a total of `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables and `r nrow(ny_noaa)` data entries. In regards to the number of missing data entries, there are a total of `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa))` values, which is `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa)) / (ncol(ny_noaa) * nrow(ny_noaa)) * 100` percent of the whole dataset. Now, we can do some data cleaning,
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  separate(date, into=c("year", "month", "day"), sep="-", remove=TRUE) |> 
  mutate(
    year = as.double(year),
    month= as.double(month),
    day = as.double(day)
  )

```
Looking at the data, we've made years, months, and days separate. Looking at the observations for temperature, the values vary between `r min(pull(ny_noaa_clean, tmin), na.rm=TRUE)` and `r max(pull(ny_noaa_clean, tmax), na.rm=TRUE)`, so the units are likely to be in Fahrenheit. For the precipitation, we have a range from `r min(pull(ny_noaa_clean, prcp), na.rm=TRUE)` and `r max(pull(ny_noaa_clean, prcp), na.rm=TRUE)`, so it could be units like cubic millimeters, or another small base unit. For snowfall, we have one column for snow and one column for snwd, which likely implies snow depth. The first observation might be new snow gained today and the second may be total snow depth, but would require more clarification. For snowfall, the most commonly observed value is `r arrange(count(ny_noaa_clean, snow), desc(n))[1,1]`, which makes sense as most of the seasons do not have snowfall.

Next, we can make a plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years.

```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |> 
  group_by(year, month) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm=TRUE), .groups= "drop"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y=mean_tmax, color=month)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temperature (°C)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month)
```

As we can see, there are no observable structure or datapoints for any max temperature in Janurary or July across each year. 

Now, for a two-panel plat showing tmax and tmin for the full dataset:

```{r}
plot1 = ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y=tmax)) + 
  geom_hex(bins = 30) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(
    title = "Max vs. Min Temperature",
    x = "Min Temp",
    y = "Max Temp",
  ) 

plot2 = ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow), snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=factor(year), y=snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust=1))
  
(plot1 + plot2)
```



# Problem 2


We load, tidy, and organize the dataset below:

```{r}
accel_data = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv",
            na = c("NA", ".", "")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to= "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(minute)
  )


demo_data = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv",
           skip=4,
           na = c("NA", ".", "")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female"
    ),
    sex = as.factor(sex),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
    ),
  education = factor(
    education,
    levels=c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")
  )) |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education)

accel_data = filter(accel_data, seqn %in% pull(demo_data, seqn))

```

To clean and tidy these datasets, we first load them in using `read_csv` and then set the na values and skip rows if needed. Then, for the accelerometer data, we use `pivot_longer` to change all of the column names from min1 to min1440 to a single variable for minutes and a separate column for the values, and ensure all of the typing is correct. For the demographic data, we case match for the sex and then filter for anyone under the age of 21 and with any NA demographic characteristics. Lastly, we filter out the accelerometer dataset for anyone who was removed from the demographic dataset. 

Now we create a table for the number of men and women in the study in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category.

```{r}
table1 = demo_data |> 
  mutate(
    ) |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) 

table1 |> knitr::kable(digits = 1)

plot3 =  
  demo_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill=sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education)

plot3
```


Now we have created our table and plot. The table shows that there is substantially more men and women who have received an education greater than high school in our dataset, with women having an education lower than high school slightly more than equivalent, and men having slightly more equivalent to high school education than lower. The plot additionally reveals that for women, there tend to me more older women with less than a high school or equivalent education while for men, there appears to be more older men with less than a high school education, but a consistent age range for equivalent education. For both men and women, there are much more younger people with a higher education compared to the older people.

Now we can create another plot for total activity for each participant, grouped by sex and education.

```{r}
total_data = accel_data |> 
  group_by(seqn) |> 
  summarize(total_activity = sum(value, na.rm=TRUE), .groups = "drop")

demo_data |> 
  mutate(
    total_activity = pull(total_data, total_activity)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=age, y=total_activity, color=sex)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education)

```

Looking at the table above, we can see that the for all three education groups, the trend lines slope downwards, which makes sense as on average, the older we get the less activity we can do. We could argue that for the less than high school education group, the trend lines are more steep than the other two groups, but I would hesitate to do so given how large the point spread/variance is.

Lastly, we create a plot of 24 hour activity time course for each education level, with color to indicate sex.

```{r}
#twenty-four hour data
tf_data = accel_data |>
  inner_join(demo_data, by="seqn") |> 
  group_by(minute, sex, education) |> 
  summarize(mean_day = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

tf_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y=mean_day, color=sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.0) +
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    y = "Activity time",
    x = "Minute",
  )
```

We initially plot this as a point/scatter plot distirbution, but due to the number of points and subsequent ambiguity, we change over to the smooth curve approximation for better clarity. We can see that for the education group, less than high school, the men and women activity time is very similar over the day, with men perhaps having slightly more activity early in the day. In the following two education groups, we can see that women have a higher activity time during the middle sections of the day, which is especially prominent in the more than high school education group.

# Problem 3

We first import, clean, and tidy the data:

```{r}
jan_2020 = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
                    na = c("NA", ".", "")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  rename(status = member_casual) |> 
  mutate(
    month = "jan", 
    year = 2020
  )

jan_2024 = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
                    na = c("NA", ".", "")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  rename(status = member_casual) |> 
  mutate(
    month = "jan", 
    year = 2024
  )

july_2020 = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv",
                    na = c("NA", ".", "")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  rename(status = member_casual) |> 
  mutate(
    month = "july", 
    year = 2020
  )

july_2024 = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv",
                    na = c("NA", ".", "")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  rename(status = member_casual) |> 
  mutate(
    month = "july", 
    year = 2024
  )

rides_data = bind_rows(jan_2020, jan_2024, july_2020, july_2024)

```

After importing the bike ride data for each month and year given, we define our na values, clean the names, rename necessary variables to more read-able values, and add a year and month column. Then we combine all datasets into one dataset with `r ncol(rides_data)` variables (cols) and `r nrow(rides_data)` rides tracked (rows). We have both identification variables like `r names(rides_data)[0:3]` and `r names(rides_data)[7:9]`, and we have ride characteristic variables like `r names(rides_data)[4:6]`. The ride during is in minutes and the station names are street intersections. The options for status are member and casual.

Below is a table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members.

```{r}
rides_data |> 
  group_by(year, month, status) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |>  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

In the table above, we can see that for each month, the number of member rides greatly exceeds the number of casual rides. For example, in January of 2020, we saw that `r count(filter(rides_data, month=="jan", year=="2020", status=="member")) / (count(filter(rides_data, month=="jan", year=="2020", status=="casual")) + count(filter(rides_data, month=="jan", year=="2020", status=="member"))) * 100` percent of rides were from members. This makes sense as riders who rode more often were more likely to be members, thus the higher total number. From 2020 to 2024, we can also see a general increase in both the number of riders, which means more people were using the bikes. We can also see that relative to each year, the number of people using the bikes in July exceeds the number in January, which makes sense as its warmer out and people are more likely to bike.

In the table below, we show the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024:

```{r}
top_5 = rides_data |> 
  filter(month == "july", year == "2024") |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(num_rides = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(num_rides)) |> 
  head(5)
top_5 |> knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```


As we can see in the table above, the ordering of the top five most popular starting stations were `r pull(top_5, start_station_name)` with the number of rides at each station being `r pull(top_5, num_rides)` respectively.

Now we can make a plot that looks at the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration:
```{r}
rides_data |> 
  filter(!is.na(duration), !is.na(weekdays)) |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels=c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday")
    ),
    year = as.character(year)
  ) |> 
  group_by(weekdays, month, year) |> 
  summarize(median_ride = median(duration, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y= median_ride, color=year)) +
  geom_point(size=3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust=1))
```


As we can see in the plot above, for each month and each year, the weekends (Saturday and Sunday) all seem to have a jump in median rides, which is understandable seeing that it is when most people are not in work, and thus have time for more leisure activities. Surprisingly, we see that July 2020 has a increase in overall median rides compared to our other three time periods, which could be related to the height of the pandemic, where people were looking for outside activities that were within the boundaries of social distancing. The other three time periods have similar patterns and median rides, with january 2020 and 2024 being slightly lower than the july 2024, which could be due to the colder weather.

Lastly, we have a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration:

```{r}
rides_data |> 
  filter(year== "2024", !is.na(duration), duration < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=duration, color=rideable_type)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_grid(month ~ status)
```

Taking a look at these plots, we can see that for casual members, they often took longer duration rides, for both the electrical and classic bikes. Even more so, we can see a slightly lower density at smaller durations for the classical bikes and higher densities for the medium duration. For the members, we can see they mostly took shorter rides, for both electrical bikes and classic bikes, and a similar overall density distribution between the two bike types. This makes sense as with a membership and lower costs per bike ride, they are more inclined to take short bike rides instead of maximizing the duration to cost ratio as a non-member would. Between July and January, there are small differences, but nothing large enough that I would note it as statistically significant.
